I am 62 years old and have farmed these fields in Quzhou for over forty years. My husband passed away some years ago, and now I make the decisions myself with help from my son when he is back from working in the city. We have five mu of good flat land with a well for irrigation. I finished middle school, so I can read the seed packets and fertilizer instructions the agro-technician gives us.

I will grow winter wheat and summer maize on the same five mu this year, just like I have always done. The wheat went in last October — I used Jimai 22, an improved variety that does well here — and now it is waking up after the winter. I will rotary-till the maize plot in late May to prepare for June planting, but for the maize itself I will use no-tillage right after cutting the wheat; that saves time and keeps the soil moisture when the summer heat comes. For maize I will plant Denghai 605, a hybrid seed I buy from the supply shop in town. The yield is much better than the old local varieties, and the grain buyer pays a fair price for it.

For fertilizer, I will put down compound fertilizer as a basal dose for both crops — about 100 jin per mu for wheat and 80 jin per mu for maize — and then topdress the wheat with urea at green-up and jointing stage because it needs extra nitrogen to fill the grain. I will irrigate the wheat four times: once now in early spring, again at jointing, at heading, and once more at grain filling if the weather stays dry. The maize will need two good irrigations, one right after sowing and one at the big-flare stage. I spray pesticides about three times per crop — herbicide once early, and insecticide twice when the worms show up. I expect the wheat to give me around 1,000 jin per mu and the maize about 1,100 jin per mu if the weather cooperates.
